Financial planning · Rate conventions · Visual planning guide

The rate says 5%. Which compounding convention turns it into a monthly payment?

Four graphics compare nominal rate conventions with an already-effective annual interpretation, then follow the converted rate through interest and principal repayment.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 4 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Translate the annual quote before calculating the monthly payment

Interactive planning lab

Effective annual interest from the selected nominal quote5.06%
Monthly payment under the selected convention$1,744.81
Payment difference versus nominal monthly compounding-$8.96

Three interpretations of the same entered annual rate number, not three current offers. A nominal quote j with m compounding periods has annual growth factor (1 + j/m)^m. Its equivalent monthly rate is that factor raised to 1/12, minus one. An already-effective annual quote uses (1 + j)^(1/12) − 1 instead. Each loan has the same principal and full repayment horizon, constant converted monthly interest, no fees and a capped final payment. The rate is assumed unchanged for the entire displayed horizon; an actual mortgage term can be much shorter than its amortization. Compounding frequency and monthly payment frequency are separate. The numerical effective annual rate here is an interest-conversion measure, not an all-in APR disclosure or a loan-eligibility result. Day-count rules, leap years, dated accrual, renewals, penalties and other charges are excluded.

The central idea

The number and the convention belong together. Convert them to a common annual growth factor and a matching payment-period rate before comparing the payment.

01

Read the convention before dividing the rate by twelve

An annual percentage printed beside the word interest does not tell you every detail needed for a payment calculation. The quotation needs a compounding convention, and the payment schedule needs a rate for its own period.

FCAC’s sample fixed-mortgage information box illustrates interest compounded twice a year but charged monthly. It also presents annual percentage rate separately, including applicable fees. The example is useful for understanding the labels; its figures are not a current mortgage offer.

This tool places three interpretations of one entered number side by side: a nominal quote with the selected compounding count, a nominal quote compounded monthly, and a number treated as already effective for one year. They share a principal and complete repayment horizon, with no fees. None is asserted to be the convention used by every lender or product.

02

Build the annual growth factor, then translate to a payment month

For a nominal annual rate j compounded m times a year, the annual growth factor is (1 + j ÷ m)m. Subtract one to obtain the effective annual interest rate. Rates in this equation are decimals, so 5% is entered as 0.05.

The equivalent monthly rate is (1 + j ÷ m)m ÷ 12 − 1. This preserves the same annual growth factor across twelve equal model months. A nominal rate compounded twice yearly is therefore converted with an exponent of one-sixth after dividing the quote by two.

If the entered number is already an effective annual rate, the monthly conversion is (1 + j)1/12 − 1. Dividing by twelve instead would make a different assumption. The tool retains unrounded rates for calculations; rounding an intermediate rate can change a long amortization schedule.

03

Compare the same rate number without assuming the same interest

With the original 5% input, nominal twice-yearly compounding implies an effective annual rate of 5.0625%. Nominal monthly compounding implies approximately 5.11619%. The already-effective annual interpretation is exactly 5%. The first chart displays the conversions on the same effective annual basis.

For an original CAD 300,000 principal repaid through three hundred monthly payments, the corresponding payments are approximately CAD 1,744.81, CAD 1,753.77 and CAD 1,734.41. These are original mathematical results, not three borrowing offers.

The same-number comparison deliberately changes economic rates. It should not be read as a claim that compounding creates extra cost when effective annual rates are held equal. If two quotes are first converted to the same annual growth factor, they also produce the same equivalent monthly rate and payment under the remaining common assumptions.

04

Carry the converted rate through the actual interest and principal split

The second chart shows additional cumulative interest relative to treating the entered number as an already-effective annual rate. Subtracting the same baseline makes a small convention difference easier to see. A zero line means equal cost to that baseline, not that the loan charges no interest. Each case solves its own payment to repay the same principal over the same number of months, with no rate renewal.

The third chart examines payment one. Interest is opening principal times the converted monthly rate. The remainder of the payment reduces principal. The final payment is capped at the amount still owed so that a small rounding residual is not treated as a new debt.

The fourth chart translates selected nominal annual quotes across annual, twice-yearly, monthly and 365-period compounding. It shows effective annual percentages to two decimal places, with more precision retained inside the calculation. The 365-period row is a mathematical count, not a dated daily-accrual contract; it does not address leap years or an actual day-count rule.

05

An effective interest conversion still does not include every borrowing cost

Converting interest conventions is one part of comparing borrowing. A real offer can also have fees, required conditions, optional products, repayment restrictions, early-exit costs or a rate that changes before the debt is fully repaid. Those are outside this exercise.

The complete repayment horizon in the tool is not a promise that a mortgage rate remains fixed for its whole amortization. Actual contractual terms and renewals must be checked separately. The calculated effective annual interest rate is also not an all-in APR disclosure: no fee has been included in its cash flows.

  1. Record the quoted number and whether it is nominal or effective.
  2. Record the compounding and payment frequencies separately.
  3. Translate to a common annual growth factor.
  4. Use the matching payment-period rate for the repayment calculation.
  5. Add actual fees and contractual terms before assessing a live offer.

These steps explain why two calculators can disagree while displaying the same annual number. Before changing the principal or repayment budget to force agreement, check whether they used the same rate convention.
